text_narrative: Halfway up the bank the fire went dull, and Odell put her hand flat on the cab side to feel the beat of the exhaust. Too soft. The blastpipe cap had been set wide at the shed that morning, and the draught through the tubes was thin enough that the coal on the front bars lay grey. She notched up, waited two chimneys, and let the damper down instead.
text_nonnarrative: Thin draught counts as a fault of the blastpipe cap and not of the coal. Where the exhaust beat is soft and the fire on the front bars stays grey, the class is one of cap setting; grate air admitted at the damper is a separate class, independent of the first. Tube condition bears on the cause and never on the class. Shed practice fixes the margin between the two.

text_narrative: A works train on the branch below Hallem overruns its stopping mark by nine coach lengths. The driver, a man of fourteen years on the section, reports that the blocks bite for the first two applications and then go slack under the shoe. Wood dust lies along the ballast for half a chain. The train stands until a fitter walks up from the yard and finds one hanger seized.
text_nonnarrative: Overrun past the stopping mark was classed by the number of applications and not by the distance. Loss of bite beyond the second application counted as block fade; a seized hanger was a defect of the shoe gear, disqualifying whatever the wood dust on the ballast showed. Driver report bore on the cause and never on the class. Train weight set the margin at which fade was allowed at all.

text_narrative: Nobody on the Pentre single line will take a token from Rees Bowen without looking at it twice, and there is a reason for that. One wet night he hands up the wrong pouch to a goods, keeps the right one in his other hand, and does not notice for eleven minutes. The goods stands at the loop with its lamp out, and the signalman there sends a boy back on foot.
text_nonnarrative: Irregular working on a single line was graded by which token was out of the instrument and not by how long it stood out. A goods held at the loop with the wrong pouch was one class; a right token left in the signalman's hand was a second, independent of it. The lamp and the boy sent back bore on the remedy and never on the grade. Minutes lost fixed neither.

text_narrative: The turntable at the old shed turned too easily for its age, and the fitter did not like to say so. Forty tons of engine on the deck and it still crept a quarter turn on its own after the pins dropped. Somebody had balanced it, that was all. Somebody who had known the pit better than anyone now alive, and who had left the handles polished at one end only.
text_nonnarrative: Out-of-balance on a turntable is a matter of load position, not of deck wear. An engine standing off centre by more than a foot is one class of fault; slack in the centre pins is a second, unaffected by the first. Handle effort at the rim is evidence of both and decisive for neither. Pit drainage bears on the cause, not the class; shed age and the tons carried are no part of it.

text_narrative: Kesh rode the survey trolley over the same eight curves four nights running. On the first night the outer rail read low by a thumb's width and the trolley leaned wrong at the exit. On the second the gauge arm froze. On the third she found the same curve high, and wrote nothing down. On the fourth the settling had gone the other way again, and she stopped trusting the arm.
text_nonnarrative: Deficient cant was classed by the difference between the two rails and not by the comfort of the ride. A curve whose outer rail stood low by more than a set width fell into the first class; a gauge arm reading falsely on the trolley was a defect of the instrument, never a class of curve. Settling of the ballast at the exit bore on the cause. Survey frequency was not a criterion.

text_narrative: There was a boilersmith in the marsh country who could hear a broken stay through the water. He would put his ear to the wrapper plate, and the cracked one would answer him a half-tone flat while all its neighbours rang true. The marsh people said he had bought the ear from something under the peat. He never denied it, and he never took payment in coin, only in salt.
text_nonnarrative: Stays tie the inner firebox to the outer wrapper across the water space. Their spacing is a function of plate thickness and of the pressure the box is to hold. Each stay is in tension only, so the two plates are independent of each other in bending. Nuts at both ends are a feature of the older pattern; the later kind is riveted over. Sound, not sight, gives the state of a stay.

text_narrative: In the third winter of the Directory's gauge order, the northern lines were required to run both brakes on one train. The Halgren mail left with vacuum on the front eight vehicles and air on the rear four, and a through pipe joined by a fitting made that week in the works. At the second stop the fitting parted, and the mail was divided for the remaining forty miles.
text_nonnarrative: Two braking systems stand opposed in the source of their effort. One holds a partial vacuum in a train pipe, so that atmospheric pressure on a piston does the work; the other holds compressed air in reservoirs under each vehicle. Cylinder size on the first is a function of the vacuum obtainable and of nothing else. Neither pipe couples to the other without a translating valve, and the two are otherwise independent.

text_narrative: When the first wheels were given out, three smiths were sent to cut their edges. The eldest cut a cone, and her wheels held the road but wore themselves hollow. The second cut a hollow, and her wheels ran true one season and climbed the rail the next. The youngest cut nothing at all, and left the rim flat, and it was her wheels that the world afterwards had to be built around.
text_nonnarrative: Three tyre profiles are usually distinguished, and the flat one is the odd member. A coned tread is separated from a flat tread by the taper across its width, which gives a rolling radius that varies with lateral position. A hollow tread is not a third design but a coned tread past its wear limit. The flange is common to all three and no part of the distinction between them.

text_narrative: Four times that autumn the keeper at the upper gate argued about the same wagon. Once it came through empty and paid nothing. Once it came loaded with hides and paid at the heavy rate. The third time the driver had swung two wheels off and dragged the bed on poles, and claimed the sledge rate. The fourth time he brought a written ruling from the trustees, folded small, and said nothing.
text_nonnarrative: Sledges make the awkward class at a toll gate, and everything else divides cleanly. Wheeled vehicles are separated from beasts under load by the count of wheels, not by weight; among wheeled vehicles the narrow tread pays above the broad, on the ground that one cuts a road and the other rolls it. A sledge has no wheels and is not a beast, so its rate is a matter of custom.

text_narrative: Rain on the hump lamps, and the man in the cabin does not look up. Wagons come over the crest one at a time and go their own ways down into the fan of sidings, each with a number chalked on its side in wet blue. Halfway down the third road a cut of four stands where nothing should stand. He puts his hand on the retarder lever and leaves it there.
text_nonnarrative: The yard lay on a fall of one in eighty from the crest to the fan of sidings. Twenty-eight roads spread below, the longest on the eastern side, the shortest against the boundary wall. Retarder rails stood on the first two hundred feet of each road. Lamps were set at the crest and nowhere further down, so the lower half of the yard was dark ground with no fixed marks on it.

text_narrative: Everyone who works the north slip knows to watch the fourth ramp plate, and they will tell a stranger so before he drives on. Old Marek keeps a bar of chalk in his coat and marks the seam when the tide is low. One market morning a hay cart goes over it wrong and sits there with its axle on the plate, and the whole slip waits for the water instead.
text_nonnarrative: Two slipways face each other across the narrows, and neither is straight. The northern one is graded at one in twelve for its upper length and one in nine below the low-water mark. Its surface is ramp plates of six feet, laid crosswise, with open seams at every joint. Weed is thickest on the lowest four plates and absent above them. The southern slip is shorter, steeper, and dry at all states of tide.

text_narrative: There was a fox who lived in a cutting and judged the trains by the noise of their wheels. A quiet wheel meant a full larder somewhere down the line, and a squealing one meant a wagon that would be set aside at the next yard, with straw in it. The badger below her said the noise was only the flange rubbing. The fox went on eating and the badger went on being right.
text_nonnarrative: Flange wear varies more between wagons on one route than between routes. The median loss on the returns is a sixteenth of an inch in a season, and a tenth of the fleet accounts for most of the spread. Inspectors on the northern district report squeal on a quarter of the vehicles they see; those in the south, on rather fewer. Curve radius explains less of the variation than most of them expect.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the trust, the surveyor laid four hundred tons of broken stone on the mile below the common. The stone was broken to a two-inch ring and spread in three layers, the last watered and rolled. By the autumn quarter the crown of that mile stood nine inches above the channels, and the trustees ordered the same on the mile above, and voted the surveyor a coat.
text_nonnarrative: Between neighbouring counties the crown of a road is more alike than between two miles of the same parish. Half the mileage in the returns has a crown of six to ten inches, and the median depth of metalling is seven. Stone size matters more to the spread than the number of layers does. Surveyors questioned on the point are divided about equally, and a third give no depth at all.

text_narrative: The overflow is running again, and Vasi knows what it will sound like before she opens the cab door. Not water. Something with a grain in it, like sand poured on tin. Three sheds on the line have reported the same and all three have been told it is air in the feed. She holds the steam valve at a quarter and listens to the cone swallow, and thinks about the well.
text_nonnarrative: An injector was a feed device without moving parts, characterised by three cones in series and an overflow to atmosphere. Its lowest working rate was a function of steam pressure and of feed-water temperature; above a certain warmth of the water it would not pick up. The overflow stood open where the jet was unformed and closed by a clack where it was not. Delivery was therefore narrow and fixed by the cone bores.

text_narrative: A grip car on the eastern incline of Tessin Station lost its hold on the cable for eleven seconds during the second shift. The operator, a woman rated for both inclines, brought the jaws off and on again twice before they took. Ninety passengers were aboard. Station engineers attributed the slip to a splice passing through the jaw, and the car was withdrawn for the remainder of the cycle.
text_nonnarrative: A grip is a clamp carried under a car and closed by hand on a moving cable, which runs at one constant speed in a slot below the road. Its holding force depends on jaw pressure and on the lay of the strands. Partial closure gives a deliberate slip and is the only speed control the car has. Splices are thicker than the standing rope and set the jaw opening.

text_narrative: The gauge stick came out of the office already broken, so the inspector held it against the headstock and read from a mark he had cut himself. Three and a half above rail on the front wagon, two and three-quarters on the one behind it. He wrote both figures on the chalk board by the weighbridge and stood looking at the pair of them while the shunter waited with his pole.
text_nonnarrative: Buffer centres are to stand between three feet five and three feet six above rail level on an empty vehicle. A lower figure is permitted only where the vehicle is restricted to one yard. Faces are required to be flat, of not less than eleven inches diameter, and set at equal heights on the two headstocks. No wagon outside these limits is to be marshalled next to a loaded one.

text_narrative: They still talk in the north shed about the fortnight the washout plugs were left alone. A foreman called Idris kept the same engine in traffic through both weeks because nothing else would hold the Tuesday goods, and he signed the book each time as if the job had been done. When the plugs finally came out there was scale in the bottom of the barrel deep enough to stand a spoon in.
text_nonnarrative: Washout is to fall due at intervals not exceeding a fortnight in hard-water districts and a month elsewhere. Plugs in the firebox crown are required to be drawn on every occasion; those in the barrel bottom, on alternate ones. Hot washing is permitted only where a supply above blood heat is laid on. An engine whose interval is exceeded is not to stand in traffic, whatever the state of the boiler.

text_narrative: There was a king who would not have his roads speak, and so the gradient posts in his country were made blank. A carter's daughter cut the true figures into the back of each one with a nail, working at night, and the carters learned to read the reverse side. When the king's men turned the posts round to face the road, the figures faced the fields, and the carters read them anyway.
text_nonnarrative: Every change of gradient is to be marked by a post carrying two arms, each inscribed with the rate of the length it points along, and a level arm between them. Arms are required to be set at four feet above rail and to read from the driving side. Posts on falling lengths steeper than one in seventy are permitted an added plate. Nothing shorter than a chain is to be posted at all.

text_narrative: In the fourth year after the Concordat took the northern boxes into public hands, the frame at Merrow Junction was rebuilt with ninety levers and a locking bed of flat bars. The old frame had held forty. On the second Sunday of the change a pilotman worked the junction by hand while the fitters cut the new bars, and the box was silent from the first light until the evening goods.
text_nonnarrative: Mechanical interlocking is best understood as a machine for making certain thoughts unthinkable. The reason is in the locking bed: a bar that will not move is not an instruction to a signalman but a limit on what his hand can do, and no attention is required of him for it to hold. Against this it is urged that any frame can be defeated by enough force. So it can, and the point stands.

text_narrative: Four hours out and the near leader is pulling short again. Sabine can feel it through the reins as plainly as if the horse were talking, and she has said so twice to the yard and been given the same answer twice. The team is to be rotated, they say. As though the team were four of a kind, as though the little mare were not carrying the whole stage alone every second journey.
text_nonnarrative: Stage horses are worked in fixed teams for a reason that has little to do with the horses. Uniform teams simplify the accounting: a stage's cost is a matter of animals per mile, and animals that cannot be interchanged make the figure impossible to keep. It is objected that individual animals differ in pull and should be matched accordingly. They do differ, and the objection makes no difference to the ledger.

text_narrative: A stone on the lower turnpike reads eleven to the town in one direction and nine in the other, and the two figures cannot both be right. A clerk of the district measures the road with a chain over two days and makes it ten and a quarter. The stone is of the same batch as its neighbours and shows no recutting. No record of the setting survives in the trust minute books.
text_nonnarrative: Milestones were worse evidence of distance than their solidity suggested. The reason was that each was cut to a measure taken from somewhere, and the somewhere was rarely written down: a market cross on one road, a bridge parapet on the next, a gate that had since gone. Defenders of the stones held that consistency mattered more than accuracy. Consistency was exactly what a stone shared with nothing beyond its own trust.

text_narrative: Rain had got into the joint again and the plates showed a rust line where the bolt heads had been slack. Aurel worked along the six of them with the long spanner, feeling for the one that would turn too far. The fourth turned three whole flats before it took up, and the plate under it had a bright crescent worn into the face where the rail had been moving all winter.
text_nonnarrative: Fishing surface: the inclined faces of the rail head and foot on which a joint plate bears. Fishing angle: the angle between those two faces, a property of the section and not of the plate. Slack joint: a joint in which the bolt tension is below the figure fixed for the section. Bright crescent: the polished mark on a plate face at a slack joint. Nip: tension in a bolt at rest.

text_narrative: Nobody would ride the middle seat of the Tessel coach after the springs were changed, and the drivers would not say why beyond the one thing. The new leather braces were quiet. Too quiet, the way a room is quiet when somebody has stopped breathing in it. A guard called Havel counted the road joints one dark stage by feel alone and reached the top of the hill four joints short.
text_nonnarrative: Thoroughbrace: a leather strap, built up of layers, from which a body was slung rather than sprung. Perch: the longitudinal beam between the two axle beds. Cee spring: a scroll of steel standing at the corner, from which braces were hung. Dead axle: an axle with no spring between it and the body. Whip: the vertical movement of a slung body, distinct from the roll about its long line.

text_narrative: There was a fireman who bet his dinner that he could fill a tender from the troughs without wetting the roof of the coach behind. He dropped the scoop at the right post and held it down one count too long, and the water came up over the tank in a sheet and stood on the coach roof like a lid. He ate his dinner in the shed with his back to the door.
text_nonnarrative: Trough: a shallow open channel laid between the rails on a level length, filled from a tank at one end. Scoop: the hinged pipe under a tender, lowered into that channel. Ramp: the graded end of a trough, outside the working depth. Pick-up length: the distance over which delivery is possible at a given speed. Overtop: water above the tank coamings, counted as waste. Coaming: the raised lip round a tank top.

text_narrative: In the sixth year of the cut, the company's gauging dock was built at the second lock and every boat on the water was called to it in turn. Weights of a hundredweight were put aboard in tens, and the freeboard read at four points on each side. The boat of a carrier named Wenn was found to have been lengthened since her registry, and her old table of indexes was burnt at the dock.
text_nonnarrative: Registered index meant, under this part, the depth of immersion set against a stated burden in the table issued to a boat. A boat whose hull was altered in length, breadth or depth was to be regauged, and her former table was of no effect. Where a reading fell between two indexes, the lower burden was taken. Nothing in this part affected the tonnage entered for a boat under any other head.

text_narrative: The gates at the lane crossing swing shut on their own about four in the afternoon, and Doriel has stopped fighting them. Nobody drives that lane. The wheel in the hut turns anyway, seven and a half revolutions, the same as if a hand were on it, and the lamps show red to a road that has been grass for thirty years. Perhaps the crossing is keeping its own hours now.
text_nonnarrative: Under this part a public carriage road crossing on the level was any highway crossed by rails otherwise than by a bridge. Gates at such a crossing were to be kept closed across the road except while a vehicle was passing, and closed across the rails at no time. Where the road was a footway only, a wicket sufficed. No provision of this part touched crossings on private occupation ways.

text_narrative: Two hundred flat tin footwarmers are drawn out of the flooded shed at Kelm Halt and carried up to the settlement on the embankment. The salts inside forty of them still take heat from boiling water and hold it about six hours. A woman keeping the stores at the halt records the good ones by the mark on the lid. The remainder are stacked in the booking hall against the wall.
text_nonnarrative: A footwarmer means, in this part, a portable vessel charged with heated water or with a salt that gives out heat on melting, and issued for the use of passengers. Where a vehicle is provided with fixed heating from the locomotive, footwarmers are not required in it. A vessel charged with anything that burns is not a footwarmer. Nothing here affects the provision of rugs, which stands under another head.

text_narrative: Before the hills were given their gradients, the makers set a small mouth in every rising road, turned against the fall. Whatever came down without a hand on it was to be taken there and laid in the ballast, and whatever came up was to pass over and feel nothing. The first runaway wagon in the world went into such a mouth and was never afterwards found, and the road above it kept its name.
text_nonnarrative: No train was in a legal position on the rising length while a catch point behind it stood closed. A trailing point set for the sand drag was the normal position, and any other position was a temporary one requiring a hand on the lever. A vehicle standing foul of the drag was not a train and could not be signalled. Reversing the point for a following movement was not permitted while the first stood on the length.

text_narrative: In the age when the cities were first strung with wire, each car carried a single arm to the sky and drew its life from a line it could not see. The rule the makers left was that no arm might leave the wire and return to it in the same place. One car's arm did, at the crossing of two lines, and the whole quarter went dark for as long as a bell takes to sound.
text_nonnarrative: A car was in a permitted state only where its pole bore on the wire from below with the spring loaded. Trailing the pole against the direction of travel was the sole legal attitude; a pole leading was an illegal state whatever the tension. At a frog or crossing the two wires counted as one, and a pole on neither was not a fault of the car. Turning a pole under load was not allowed.

text_narrative: Twice in the spring and once again in the autumn, Grelis took the wooden bow gauge round the same three bridges. In the spring the bow passed everything but the flat wagon with the boiler on it. In the second week the boiler had gone and the bow caught on a sheet rail nobody had reported. In the autumn the bridge itself had been packed up an inch, and the bow would not go through at all.
text_nonnarrative: A load was in an allowable position only where every part of it lay inside the profile fixed for the route. Height above rail and width at each height were both binding, and satisfying one did not license the other. A load fouling the profile at one bridge alone was out of gauge for the whole route. Sheets and ropes counted as part of the load, and the wagon's own fittings did not either.

text_narrative: Six felloe blanks stand against the wall of the shop, cut across the grain of an elm that came down in the autumn. The old wheelwright sets the first on the block, marks it from the tracing board with a nail, and takes the outside down in four passes of the adze. Her apprentice holds the tail. The shaving off the last pass is as long as the bench and does not break.
text_nonnarrative: Felloe stock in a country shop was elm, ash and beech, of which elm was the commonest and the least regular. Each blank was a segment of about a sixth of the circle, two and a half inches thick, with the grain following the curve. Ash blanks were lighter and reserved for light traps; beech was scarce and used where a wheel was to stand in water. Nothing was cut from oak at all.

text_narrative: They kept one lamp in the Ardvey lamp room that nobody would trim, and it stood at the end of the shelf with its number turned to the wall. Lampmen said the wick came out of it wet whatever the weather. A relief man trimmed it once because he had not been told, and put it out on the down starter, and the lamp burned four nights on a fill that should have done one.
text_nonnarrative: Three patterns of oil lamp were held in a lamp room, and the smallest was the most numerous. Signal lamps were the bulk of the stock, each with a single flat wick, a fount of about a pint, and a spectacle plate outside the glass. Handlamps were fewer, with three shades in one case. Gauge lamps were two only, kept apart on the top shelf, and were the sole pattern with a chimney.

text_narrative: There was a mason who would build no parapet higher than a horse's knee, and the village called her mean with stone. She said a pannier needs air on both sides and a horse needs to see the water. Long after, when a cart tried the bridge and stuck, they sent for her and she was gone, and the low walls stayed as she left them for another hundred years.
text_nonnarrative: What was usually praised in the packhorse bridge was the wrong thing. Its admirers took the low parapet for humility of design, when it was a clearance dimension and nothing else. The narrowness was likewise read as poverty, though a single file of animals needed no more. The best of these bridges were the ones whose spans followed the rock rather than the road, and those were seldom the ones drawn.

text_narrative: In the second summer of the lines, the observation section put up four balloons a day from three fields. Each was held on a steel cable from a winch lorry and worked to a thousand feet, with a telephone wire twisted along the cable. On the ninth of that month the wind at height turned and the northern balloon lay over so far that the observer in the basket could see only cloud.
text_nonnarrative: Accounts of tethered observation were written almost entirely about the balloon and hardly at all about the winch, and that was the error of the literature. Height was the figure quoted, though what governed the usefulness of a station was cable behaviour in wind. Sceptics answered that the two could not be separated. They could not, which was why the better accounts were those written by winch crews rather than observers.

text_narrative: The engine has a limp in it and Halloran cannot find a name for what is wrong. Not the rods themselves. The rods are true, he has had them off and on the marking table, and the crank pins measure what they should. So the fault is in a relation and not in a thing, which is no use at all to a man writing a repair card at two in the morning.
text_nonnarrative: Quartering was a property of no part of an engine taken alone. Whether it counted as a dimension was disputable: a dimension belonged to a piece, and this belonged to the angle between two pieces, each of which could be correct while the pair was wrong. If such relations were dimensions, then a machine had properties that no measurement of its parts could reach. If not, the word was too narrow for the workshop.

text_narrative: A district engineer's return from the western section lists sleeper spacing at two figures for the same mile, twenty-four inches and twenty-six, and gives no reason for the difference. The section foreman, asked at the office, says the spacing was set to the timber available in the year the length was relaid. Records for that year are missing. The mile carries the same traffic as its neighbours and shows no more wear.
text_nonnarrative: Spacing was treated as a specification, but it was closer to a residue. A specified quantity was one chosen for a reason that could be stated; sleeper spacing on most lines was whatever the timber and the practice of a district had left. If a residue of that kind counted as a specification, then everything in a permanent way was specified and the word was idle. If it did not, half the standards were misnamed.

text_narrative: When the roads of iron were laid across the plain, the makers were told to leave a shoulder of stone beyond each end of every sleeper, and the width of it was fixed by a measure nobody was shown. Where the shoulder was full, the road held its line through the floods of that age. Where it had been robbed for a wall, the line went crooked and the wall did not stand either.
text_nonnarrative: Lateral resistance of a sleeper stands roughly in proportion to the shoulder width beyond its end, up to a limit of about a foot. Past that width the added stone contributes nothing measurable, the constant of proportionality being a property of the stone's angle of repose rather than of the sleeper. Depth under the sleeper enters a different relation altogether, and the two are not additive. Neither relation holds for a shoulder of sand.

text_narrative: Three runs up the bank on three successive days, and Ferrand uses the sand differently each time. On the first day she puts it on early and gets to the top with the box empty and the fire dull. On the second she waits and loses her feet twice within a chain. On the third she works the valve in short bursts against the low wheel, and the marker at the top drops his flag.
text_nonnarrative: Adhesion available was proportional to the weight on the driving wheels, with a coefficient that dry sand raised by about a half on a clean rail and by rather more on a greasy one. The coefficient was a property of the surfaces and not of the load, so doubling the weight doubled the tractive effort obtainable and left the ratio untouched. Beyond a certain rate of feed the relation flattened and sand was simply lost.

text_narrative: In the first days of the iron roads there was a fire that would not stay in its box, and it went out at the chimney in pieces and settled in the corn. The makers hung a net of wire inside the smokebox to keep the pieces at home. The fire learned the mesh. Wherever the wire was coarsest it went through whole, and the corn on those lengths was cut early ever after.
text_nonnarrative: The smokebox held four things besides its own shell: the tube plate at the back, the blastpipe standing on the saddle, the petticoat above it, and a netting hung between the two on a light frame. The netting was in panels, each removable through the front door. Its frame was carried on lugs riveted to the shell and touched nothing else. On the smaller classes the petticoat was absent and the netting sat lower.

text_narrative: Every market day the same three barrows go over the boards at the end of the down platform, and every market day one wheel finds the gap. The porter with the fish crate takes it slowly and gets across. The woman with the churns lifts her offside wheel over by hand. The boy with the parcels runs at it, and the barrow stops dead with the parcels going on without it.
text_nonnarrative: A barrow crossing has three parts: a ramp at each platform end, a boarded way between the rails, and a check rail on the inner face of each running rail. The boards sit level with the rail head, with a flangeway open on the gauge side. That gap is the only part with no counterpart in the platform surface. Ramps are absent where the platform is low, and the boarded way is correspondingly longer.
